summary: Proposes an SMTP service extension that works like a real-world No Soliciting sign for email, along with a new message header and additions to the Received header. It aims to let senders and recipients signal that unsolicited mail is unwelcome.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like a No Soliciting sign on your door, but for email. This document defines how the sign is posted and read.

questions: what is the smtp no-soliciting extension
what does solicit= do in mail from
how do mail servers reject unsolicited mail
subtitle: An SMTP extension that works like a No Soliciting sign: a mail server says which kinds of solicitation it does not want.

tldr.problem: Anti-spam tools mostly filter after delivery, and none of them tells a sending SMTP agent that the receiver does not want a class of solicitation.
tldr.mechanism: The NO-SOLICITING extension lets a server announce solicitation class keywords in its EHLO reply. A sender labels mail with a Solicitation: header and a SOLICIT= parameter on MAIL FROM, and intermediate MTAs can record keywords in Received: trace fields.
tldr.outcome: Unwanted mail can be refused before transfer, which saves bandwidth, disk space and processing. The extension does not deal with authentication or consent, and it defines no policy on which keywords to use.

today: RFC 3865 is a Proposed Standard from September 2004, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text leaves open which keywords are used and who must honour them, and says the extension carries no authentication or consent.

sections.title: The Problem and the Sign Analogy
sections.content:
The RFC opens by describing unsolicited bulk email (UBE), or spam, as one of the most pressing issues on the Internet. It lists existing defences: whitelists, blacklists, spam filters, technical considerations documents and "do not spam" list proposals.

It then draws on real-world "No Soliciting" signs, which municipalities and courts have generally allowed residents to post. None of the existing anti-spam proposals gives notice to an SMTP agent that is delivering mail that the receiver does not want solicitations. Such a virtual sign would let a receiving system serve notice that a class of mail is not desired, and if a message is properly labelled, the transfer can be skipped. That saves network bandwidth, disk space and processing power compared with filtering after delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: If a house has a No Soliciting sign, salespeople know not to knock. This idea gives mail servers a sign so unwanted mail is not even carried inside.

sections.title: The Three Pieces
sections.content:
The memo defines three characteristics that work together:

  • A service extension that lets a receiving Mail Transport Agent (MTA) tell the sending MTA that no soliciting is in effect.
  • A header field, Solicitation:, with which the message sender flags a message as belonging to a class.
  • An extension of trace fields so that an intermediate MTA can mark a message as belonging to a class.

The RFC says this lets "good" spammers meet labelling requirements, and gives destination MTAs something to act on when senders do not follow such conventions. It also states plainly that the extension does not deal with authentication or consent.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three parts: the sign on the door, a label on each package, and a stamp that the delivery people can add along the way.

sections.title: Solicitation Class Keywords
sections.content:
The extension is named NO-SOLICITING and is announced in the EHLO exchange, with one optional parameter: zero or more solicitation class keywords. A keyword given during the initial EHLO applies to every message in the session. Further keywords can be added per recipient in replies to RCPT TO.

Keywords are separated by commas. The initial set all begin with a domain name with its labels reversed, followed by a colon, so example.com gives com.example:. The rest uses letters, digits and the characters period, hyphen, underscore and colon. A keyword MUST be less than 1000 characters, and a whole keyword set must also stay under 1000 characters.

Any domain registrant may define a keyword, and discovery of keywords is out of scope. There is no default keyword, so a bare 250-NO-SOLICITING is a no-op that only invokes the extension. The RFC rejects a simple yes/no flag so that the mail system stays neutral and different definitions can co-exist. It does not say which keywords to use, which it calls a policy decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The sign can say which kinds of visitors are not welcome, using a name that starts with the sender's own web address backwards so nobody's names clash.

sections.title: MAIL FROM, Replies and Error Codes
sections.content:
The extension defines SOLICIT as a parameter of MAIL FROM, written SOLICIT= followed by a comma-separated keyword list with no white space. The keywords MUST be identical to those in the message's Solicitation: header, and MUST NOT be supplemented from Received: trace fields.

The receiving MTA decides per message. In the RFC's example, the server announces net.example:ADV in EHLO, and the client sends MAIL FROM:<save@example.com> SOLICIT=org.example:ADV:ADLT. The first recipient is accepted with 250. The second is refused with 550, and the reply echoes the matching keywords. A rejecting MTA SHOULD declare its keywords in EHLO or per recipient, and SHOULD NOT deliver a message whose Solicitation: matches one it declared.

If Enhanced Mail Status Codes are in use, the usual code for such a rejection is 5.7.1. Other codes, including temporary ones, may fit better, for example when size limits are applied by class.
sections.plainLanguage: When a sender says what is in its package, the receiving server can say "yes, drop it off" for one person and "no, not for this person" for another, and explain why.

sections.title: The Solicitation Header, Trace Fields and Relays
sections.content:
The new header looks like Solicitation: net.example:ADV,org.example:ADV:ADLT: the name, one or more spaces, then keywords. The RFC prefers it over putting keywords in Subject:, because a subject line gives cues to people but not a straightforward signal to programs. The header could even be inserted automatically by the sender's mail client.

Only the sending client can set that header, and intermediate MTAs may change only Received:. So the RFC adds a way to put keywords in a Received: comment, for example by foo-mta.example.com with ESMTP (SOLICIT=net.example:ADV,org.example:ADV:ADLT). Trace keywords may disagree with the header, so implementors SHOULD examine the header and MAY examine trace keywords.

The extension applies to relayed mail too. A client SHOULD take the SOLICIT keywords from the header and check their syntax. A server SHOULD set the parameter when it receives a message from a non-conforming MTA.
sections.plainLanguage: The package label is written by the sender. Delivery trucks cannot change it, but they can add a sticker saying what they noticed on the way.

sections.title: Defaults, Consent and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says implementations SHOULD NOT enable specific solicitation classes by default, and administrators SHOULD NOT turn on extra per-recipient filtering for users by default. It gives the reason that some policy makers may see default filtering as a prior restraint on commercial speech. How a user asks for filtering is out of scope.

The security section is short and candid. The extension provides no authentication of senders and does not say when a sender should use it or whether consent was given. A sender might therefore treat a receiver's lack of the extension as consent, so the RFC states that non-use of NO-SOLICITING by a receiving MTA SHALL NOT indicate consent.
sections.plainLanguage: Not having a sign on your door never means you invited salespeople in.
